title: Flowers on the Wrench
hook: night nine: auto-rickshaws wear garlands, a mechanic puts a flower on his wrench, and the last name in the list is the giver of accomplishment
carry: work offered to God becomes worship
tomorrow: can anyone find the end of a pillar of fire?

segments.voice: Yesterday, night eight: the goddess dwells in every being, served in young girls at the table. Tonight, the last night.

An auto-rickshaw parked outside a temple, with a garland of marigolds across its windshield and a smear of turmeric on the bumper. A mechanic's shop where the wrenches have been wiped clean, laid in a row and given a flower each. A tailor's sewing machine with a red dot on it. A laptop, closed, with a sprig of something green on the lid. In parts of South India, the ninth day of Navaratri is Ayudha Puja, the worship of tools. Where it's kept, the tools aren't worked with today. They're cleaned, thanked and honored.
screen: `A GARLAND ON THE WINDSHIELD.` → `A FLOWER ON EACH WRENCH.` → `TOOLS CLEANED AND HONORED.`

segments.voice: The ninth name in the Kavacha's list, the last one, is Siddhidatri, the giver of siddhi: accomplishment, the power to bring a thing to completion. On this night she's shown seated on a lotus, calm. Now put her beside the mechanic. Where does accomplishment come from? Hindus have an old answer, near the end of the Bhagavad Gita. Krishna says a person reaches siddhi, the same word, by worshiping the one from whom all beings come, through their own work. Not by leaving the shop for the temple. By the work itself, offered. That's the teaching Ayudha Puja acts out once a year. The wrench, the sewing machine, the pen, the stove, the laptop are how a life serves, so for a day they're cleaned, rested and honored like anything else on an altar. Look back over the nine nights. The goddess came as the mountain's daughter, a smile that made a world, a mother with her child, a warrior named for a sage, night itself, the bright one washed clean, and now the giver of accomplishment. And remember night one. Near the end of the Devi Mahatmya, the goddess herself speaks of the great worship offered to her in autumn, and says that whoever hears her story then, with devotion, will be freed from troubles by her grace. Tomorrow the year turns to Shiva, and to the Shiva Purana.
screen: `SIDDHIDATRI, GIVER OF ACCOMPLISHMENT.` · `THE GITA: SIDDHI THROUGH YOUR OWN WORK.` · `THE TOOLS REST ON THE ALTAR.` · `THE AUTUMN WORSHIP AND THE BOOK.` · then, large: `WORK OFFERED IS WORSHIP.`

segments.voice: One by one, bring to mind the things your hands use to get through a day, keys, a phone, a pan, a pen, a keyboard, a steering wheel, a broom, and give each a moment of thanks, the way the mechanic gives each wrench a flower. Then let the hands themselves come to mind, resting in your lap; they're tools too. If you pray, you can offer tomorrow's work to the goddess, or to God, in your own words. If you don't, simply decide to do one piece of it well, as a gift.
Navaratri, night nine: Siddhidatri, the giver of accomplishment, and the day the tools rest and are honored.
Your line: work offered to God becomes worship. A flower on every wrench. The goddess's part, complete.
